content: Post-surgical radiotherapy (RT) combined with chemotherapy is currently considered the standard treatment for children diagnosed with medulloblastoma. The introduction of chemotherapy aims to improve survival rates and mitigate the adverse effects caused by RT. In very young children, the reduction of RT-related side effects has been achieved by omitting craniospinal RT altogether. For older children, these side effects have been minimized by reducing the dose and field of craniospinal RT and limiting the boost volume to the tumor bed. The primary objectives of this study were to evaluate event-free survival (EFS), disease-free survival (DFS), and overall survival (OS) in children with medulloblastoma who received chemotherapy as part of their primary treatment compared to those who did not. Additionally, the study aimed to compare EFS, DFS, and OS in children receiving standard-dose RT without chemotherapy versus those receiving reduced-dose RT with chemotherapy. Secondary objectives included assessing the potential adverse effects of chemotherapy and RT, including long-term side effects and their impact on quality of life. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE/PubMed, and EMBASE, covering studies published up to August 2013. They also reviewed reference lists, conference proceedings, and ongoing trial databases. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the specified treatments in children aged 0 to 21 years with medulloblastoma. Seven RCTs involving 1,080 children were identified. A meta-analysis of EFS/DFS, excluding disease progression during therapy as an event, showed a statistically significant benefit for treatment including chemotherapy (hazard ratio [HR] 0.70; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.54 to 0.91; P = 0.007). However, when disease progression during therapy was included as an event, the benefit was no longer observed (HR 1.02; 95% CI 0.70 to 1.47; P = 0.93). Two individual studies using alternative definitions of EFS/DFS also failed to demonstrate a clear difference between treatment arms. Notably, in one study that excluded disease progression as an event, the initial statistical significance favoring chemotherapy disappeared with longer follow-up due to late relapses in the chemotherapy group. There was no clear evidence of a difference in overall survival (OS) between treatment arms (HR 1.06; 95% CI 0.67 to 1.67; P = 0.80). Among eight reported adverse effects, two (severe infections and fever/neutropenia) were more common in the chemotherapy group. Severe infections had a risk ratio (RR) of 5.64 (95% CI 1.28 to 24.91; P = 0.02), and fever/neutropenia was also significantly more frequent (Fisher's exact P = 0.01). Other adverse effects, such as acute alopecia, reduction in intelligence quotient, secondary malignancies, hematological toxicity, hepatotoxicity, and treatment-related mortality, showed no significant differences between treatment arms. Quality of life was not evaluated in any of the studies. Subgroup analyses based on age (younger versus older children) and risk status (high-risk versus non-high-risk) yielded inconsistent results. Only one RCT compared standard-dose RT without chemotherapy to reduced-dose RT with chemotherapy. This study found no significant difference in EFS/DFS between the groups (HR 1.54; 95% CI 0.81 to 2.94; P = 0.19). Other outcomes and subgroup analyses were not evaluated in this trial. The potential for bias could not be excluded in any of the included studies. The authors concluded that while the evidence does not definitively confirm a benefit of chemotherapy, it also does not exclude the possibility of such a benefit. Treatment outcomes must be interpreted in the context of the entire therapeutic approach, including surgery and craniospinal RT, as well as the specific chemotherapy protocols used. This review focused on the general concept of treatment rather than identifying the optimal chemotherapy agents or radiation doses. Several factors, such as the long time span between studies and changes in treatment practices, complicated the interpretation of results. The absence of significant differences between treatment arms may also be attributed to low statistical power or insufficient follow-up duration. Although RCTs represent the highest level of evidence, data from non-randomized studies suggest promising outcomes for chemotherapy-only approaches in very young children without metastatic disease. However, only one RCT addressed the comparison of standard-dose RT without chemotherapy versus reduced-dose RT with chemotherapy, precluding definitive conclusions. Further high-quality research is urgently needed.
